extracted.intended_audience: legislators, PTO officials, patent practitioners, patent applicants, and stakeholders in patent policy
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory guidance and policy provisions for proposed patent-law reforms (the America Invents Act), covering PTO-authorized programs, inequitable-conduct enforcement, novelty standards, administrative procedures, fee handling, and related procedural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary search-and-patentability program with incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10 authorizes the PTO to offer incentives to applicants who submit a search report and a patentability analysis as part of a voluntary search-and-patentability program, rather than mandating such submissions for all applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than mandate a requirement (which would be very expensive to applicants), PTO may offer incentives to encourage participation. A well-functioning and heavily used program should help PTO process backlog, discover private prior-art search costs, and test whether file-wrapper immunity works as intended in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: File-wrapper immunity for program participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution records of patents secured through the voluntary search-and-patentability program shall be inadmissible to construe patent claims in later proceedings (file-wrapper immunity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This immunity is an essential prerequisite to making the voluntary program palatable and is expected to be a strong inducement for applicants to participate; it allows applicants to speak freely with examiners without constant litigation-minded caution and reduces the incentive to over-lawyer prosecution discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO regulations identifying materials eligible for immunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed section 123(b) authorizes PTO to issue regulations identifying material submitted in an attempt to comply with the search-and-patentability program that shall receive file-wrapper immunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations should encourage applicants who might fear that aborted or failed attempts would create a record later used in litigation to limit claim scope. Such regulatory identification helps assure participants that even an unsuccessful attempt will not be used against them.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO may offer other incentives and retain existing authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed section 123(a) authorizes the PTO to offer various other incentives to parties who participate in a search-and-patentability program, and subsection 10(b) precludes the negative implication that PTO currently lacks authority to offer incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO may continue to offer incentives under existing pilots and programs without issuing new regulations; the bill is intended to allow a substantial trial run if incentives and demands are reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift inequitable-conduct enforcement to PTO administrative proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11 proposes shifting enforcement of the doctrine of inequitable conduct from civil litigation to administrative proceedings before the PTO under proposed sections 298 and 299.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the administrative framework PTO will reissue patents if needed to remove invalid claims, assess culpability for misconduct, and impose sanctions including civil fines and, in severe cases, unenforceability. This mirrors how other federal agencies police misconduct in agency proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO authority to accept complaints from broad sources, but limit defendants
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (a) of proposed section 299 authorizes the PTO to issue regulations accepting complaints from any source, but the section allows complaints to be filed only against individuals and entities that are parties to matters or proceedings before the Office (excluding examiners and PTO personnel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO may later limit who may file complaints if certain sources produce voluminous or unproductive allegations; limiting defendants reduces risk that proceedings become a de facto appeal of examiner rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO-controlled misconduct proceedings without adversarial participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings authorized by section 299 will be prosecuted by the PTO alone, without the participation of parties adverse to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO prefers to control prosecution of misconduct because the principal injury is to PTO's interest in integrity of its proceedings; patents still may be challenged in court if an owner enforces claims obtained by misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve unenforceability penalty for particularly egregious misconduct by current beneficial owner
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (b)(3)(C) of section 299 permits PTO to render a patent unenforceable as a sanction, but this penalty is reserved for particularly egregious misconduct committed by the current beneficial owner of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This elevated standard aligns with foundational Supreme Court cases (Precision Instrument, Hazel-Atlas Glass) and seeks to avoid punishing good-faith purchasers or applying an overly draconian penalty where misconduct is not directly attributable to the current owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform public-availability test for novelty (eliminate public use/on-sale bars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed section 102(a)(1) amends novelty by eliminating public use and the on-sale bar as independent bases of invalidity and instead imposes a uniform test of whether art has been made available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity determinations will be based exclusively on information available to the public, increasing certainty and predictability, and should reduce discovery (defendants need not uncover private sales or nonpublic information). The doctrine of inherency will continue to define aspects of what is publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency doctrine remains relevant to public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of what is deemed publicly available is defined in important respects by the doctrine of inherency: once a product is sold, any invention necessarily present in the product and recognizable by a person skilled in the art is deemed publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This treatment of inherency means products on the market can render inventions publicly available and unpatentable; industrialized countries using a public-availability standard have not experienced significant problems with secret commercialization followed by late patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-to-file system mitigates secret commercialization concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a first-to-file system, a manufacturer who secretly commercializes and then seeks belated patenting runs the risk that someone else might patent the invention first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This competitive incentive is cited as a reason why imposing a public-availability standard should not encourage secret commercialization followed by late patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate best-mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(c) eliminates the current law's best-mode requirement as a condition of patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any useful information from describing a best mode will be provided by satisfying written description and enablement; because best-mode turns on subjective intent and causes discovery (depositions of inventor), eliminating it will make litigation less burdensome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve small-entity opt-out of 18-month publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill preserves the current exception (opt-out) to 18-month publication for small patent owners rather than eliminating it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-business applicants use the exception to preserve market advantage and prevent foreign appropriation of inventions prior to patent issuance; about 40,000 uses annually indicate heavy reliance by small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert day-based deadlines to month-based deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: A new subsection converts various day-based deadlines in title 35 into month-based deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Month-based deadlines are easier to calculate, reduce ministerial mistakes, and save billable hours and administrative burden over the years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify CREATE Act joint-ownership prior-art interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2(b) includes a minor modification to the CREATE Act aligning its text to PTO's current interpretation regarding who must own prior art regarded as jointly owned by parties to a joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a statutory alignment to reduce disputes about ownership of prior art under joint research agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create revolving fund to prevent diversion of PTO fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 14 (Coburn amendment) would create a revolving fund so all fees paid by patent and trademark applicants and owners remain at the PTO and cannot be diverted to unrelated Government programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fee diversion has hampered PTO's ability to hire examiners and contributed to backlog and pendency; keeping fees would allow PTO to fund examinations and reduce application backlog without taxpayer money.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-level goals of the America Invents Act
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act aims to (1) improve and harmonize PTO operations; (2) improve patent quality; and (3) provide more certainty in litigation (including transition to first-inventor-to-file and greater third-party input).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These goals drive provisions such as resources for PTO, procedural reforms, first-inventor-to-file transition, and mechanisms to increase third-party engagement to separate 'inventive wheat from chaff' and promote competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address perverse effects of current inequitable-conduct doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform effort recognizes that current inequitable-conduct doctrine (asserted in majority of suits, severe 'all-or-nothing' penalty, unpredictable materiality standards) produces undesirable consequences: excessive litigation, discovery burdens, defensive floods of disclosures, or complete nondisclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifting enforcement to PTO administrative proceedings and reserving unenforceability for egregious cases aims to reduce the doctrine's chilling effect on useful disclosures and to prevent over-lawyering and counterproductive prosecution tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO discretion to manage complaint sources and burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: While PTO may accept complaints from a broad range of parties, the Office has discretion to limit sources if filings from certain types of sources prove burdensome or unproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discretion is intended to prevent misuse of complaint mechanisms and reduce administrative burdens from frivolous or tactical filings aimed at harassing parties or appealing examiner decisions indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions proportional to materiality and mens rea in PTO proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed section 299 authorizes PTO to assess the materiality of alleged misconduct and the mens rea of the malfeasant and to levy appropriate sanctions (ranging up to civil fines and, in severe cases, unenforceability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framework contemplates proportionate penalties tied to culpability and harm to PTO's processes, in contrast to blanket judicial unenforceability that may be applied under current doctrine.
